subject: Chemistry
title: Ibuprofen: The Anti-Inflammatory
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Ibuprofen: The Anti-Inflammatory.

hook.text: Stewart Adams spent 10 years developing ibuprofen. He first tested it on himself—for a hangover headache.

buildup.text: Adams at Boots UK wanted a safer alternative to aspirin. He screened over 600 compounds before finding ibuprofen in 1961.

discovery.text: Ibuprofen blocks COX enzymes that produce prostaglandins—chemicals that cause pain, fever, and inflammation.

twist.text: COX-2 inhibitors were designed to be even safer. But Vioxx caused heart attacks—and was pulled from the market in 2004.

climax.text: Ibuprofen is now sold in over 120 countries. It treats headaches, arthritis, and fever for billions of people worldwide.

punchline.text: 600 failed compounds, one hangover test. A decade of work became a household staple.

quiz.question: How does ibuprofen reduce pain and inflammation?
options: It blocks COX enzymes that produce prostaglandins causing pain and inflammation
It numbs nerve endings directly at the site of injury
It reduces blood flow to inflamed areas

details.summary: Ibuprofen reversibly inhibits cyclooxygenase enzymes COX-1 and COX-2, reducing prostaglandin production that causes pain, inflammation, and fever. Developed by Stewart Adams at Boots in 1961, it became one of the most widely used over-the-counter medications worldwide.
details.whyItMatters: Ibuprofen provides accessible pain relief for billions of people. Understanding its COX inhibition mechanism led to the development of more selective anti-inflammatory drugs with fewer side effects.
takeaways: Ibuprofen reversibly blocks both COX-1 and COX-2 prostaglandin synthesis
It reduces pain, inflammation, and fever through a single mechanism
Stewart Adams tested the first dose on his own hangover headache

faq.question: Why can ibuprofen cause stomach problems in some people?
faq.answer: COX-1 produces prostaglandins that protect the stomach lining by maintaining mucus and bicarbonate secretion. Ibuprofen inhibits both COX-1 and COX-2 non-selectively, reducing this protective mucus. Long-term use can lead to gastric erosion, ulcers, and gastrointestinal bleeding.

faq.question: How is ibuprofen different from acetaminophen and aspirin?
faq.answer: Ibuprofen reduces pain, fever, and inflammation through reversible COX inhibition. Aspirin is an irreversible COX inhibitor with stronger antiplatelet effects. Acetaminophen reduces pain and fever through a central nervous system mechanism but has virtually no anti-inflammatory action.
